narrative: Your application for admission was unfortunately rejected because our model predicts a 51.8% probability that you would not pass the bar exam on your first attempt. While your undergraduate GPA of 3.40 is actually higher than the 3.24 average of students who pass, your performance during law school—ranking in the bottom 10% to 20% of your class—suggests a significant struggle with the legal curriculum. This narrow prediction of failure is the primary reason your application cannot proceed at this time. To help you understand this decision, we looked at "what if" scenarios, which are alternative versions of your profile that would have resulted in an admission. These scenarios identify the smallest changes needed to flip the model’s prediction from a failure to a passing result. By comparing your specific background as a full-time Hispanic male student from a lower-middle-income family to these alternatives, we can see exactly where the model's sensitivity lies. We analyzed three distinct alternative scenarios, and surprisingly, the only factor that changed in every single one was your undergraduate grade point average. In all three cases, the model indicated that if your undergraduate GPA had been 3.20 instead of 3.40, you would have been predicted to pass the bar exam. Other factors, such as your LSAT score of 36.00, your family income bracket, and your full-time status, remained exactly the same across every scenario. It appears the model is identifying a specific relationship between your high undergraduate grades and your much lower law school decile rankings of 1.0 and 2.0. When these two metrics are far apart, the model may interpret the gap as a sign of academic inconsistency that increases the risk of failing the bar. Because your predicted probability of failure is so close to the threshold at 51.8%, even a minor adjustment in how your academic history is viewed would change the outcome. While you cannot change your past undergraduate GPA, this insight suggests that the model's concern isn't your intelligence, but rather the sharp decline in your performance once you reached law school. If you can provide evidence of academic growth or explain the discrepancy between your strong 3.40 undergraduate start and your later class rankings, you may be able to overcome this statistical hurdle. Ultimately, the model sees your current profile as slightly too risky because your law school rankings are significantly lower than the average passing student's rank of approximately 6.0. By narrowing that gap through further study or a higher ranking in future terms, you would likely move into the passing category. Focusing on bringing your law school performance closer to the level of your undergraduate success is the most direct path to changing this prediction.
